items.abstract_text: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

items.abstract_text: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how knowledge workers make sense of GenAI-enabled co-production, with particular attention to authorship ambiguity and its implications for competence attribution, self-evaluation and meaningful work. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative approach based on in-depth interviews with 32 knowledge workers who work directly with GenAI tools, combining inductive coding with abductive interpretation. We used the Gioia methodology to analyze participants' reported experiences and interpretations of human–AI collaboration, with sensemaking informing the interpretation of emergent themes and aggregate dimensions. Findings The findings identify authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. When GenAI contributes to ideation, analysis, drafting, coding or other knowledge-intensive outputs, workers may find it difficult to distinguish their own contribution from that of the technology. Participants responded to this ambiguity differently. Some reconstructed their expertise around judgment, validation and contextualization and experienced GenAI as extending their professional capability. Others struggled to internalize successful outputs as evidence of their own competence and reported impostor-like experiences and reduced meaningfulness. The findings suggest that experiences of GenAI-enabled co-production depend on whether workers interpret and reconstruct their contribution. Practical implications Managers in comparable knowledge-intensive settings may consider making human judgment visible, clarifying legitimate uses of GenAI and recognizing contributions beyond output speed and quality. Originality/value This study identifies authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. It shows how uncertainty regarding the respective contributions of the worker and GenAI can complicate competence attribution and initiate sensemaking about professional contribution. By explaining how workers' interpretations of authorship ambiguity are associated with divergent identity and meaning outcomes, including enhanced capability, impostor-like experiences and changing meaningfulness, the study extends research on human–AI collaboration beyond its predominant focus on performance and productivity.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Natural language processing and AI models are increasingly used to extract emotional signals from textual data; however, systematic validation of different computational paradigms in emotionally complex relational contexts remains limited. Such approaches may contribute to digital health research, particularly in the fields of digital mental health and couples therapy, where understanding emotional expressions within romantic relationships is especially relevant. Objective This study aimed to compare a lexicon-based approach (NRC Emotion Lexicon) and a transformer-based model (Pysentimiento) in detecting affective patterns within spontaneous romantic relationship narratives and to evaluate their criterion-related associations with a theory-driven measure of relational well-being. Methods In this cross-sectional exploratory study, 112 Spanish adults completed the Couple Flourishing Measure (CFM) and provided an open-ended description of their romantic relationship. Narratives were analyzed using both computational approaches to generate emotion and sentiment indices. Pearson correlations were computed between model outputs and CFM scores. Steiger Z tests were conducted to compare dependent correlations across models. Results Both approaches showed significant associations with couple flourishing, although the transformer-based model yielded stronger correlations for several affective dimensions, particularly positive sentiment ( r =0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.76) and negative sentiment ( r =−0.74, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.65). The lexicon-based approach showed smaller associations, primarily for negative emotions. Steiger Z tests identified significant between-model differences for disgust ( P =.04), joy ( P =.01), sadness ( P =.004), surprise ( P =.03), and positive and negative sentiment (both P <.001), but not for anger or fear. Conclusions In this sample, Pysentimiento showed stronger associations with couple flourishing than the NRC Emotion Lexicon across several affective dimensions, although differences were not consistent across all categories. These findings support the value of theory-driven external criteria for evaluating computational emotion detection in relational narratives and underscore the importance of context-sensitive interpretation when applying AI tools in psychologically sensitive domains. These findings also highlight the potential relevance of computational emotion analysis for digital health research, particularly in digital mental health and couples therapy research, although further validation in clinical settings is needed before clinical implementation.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background AI is increasingly embedded in health care and digital health applications, shaping clinical processes as well as how patients access information and participate in care. Research on bias in medical AI has largely focused on technical and performance-related disparities. Less attention has been paid to how such biases may affect patients’ access, understanding, trust, and opportunities for meaningful involvement in care. Objective This scoping review aimed to map how studies of bias in medical AI describe patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment and the digital divide and to identify gaps across technical, social, structural, and patient-centered perspectives. Methods This scoping review followed JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases were searched in August 2025 and supplemented by Google Scholar searches. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 onward were included if they addressed bias in medical AI and described patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment or digital inequality. Data charting focused on AI application types, bias dimensions, patient empowerment domains, digital divide–related factors, intersectionality, and debiasing strategies. Findings were synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results The search identified 497 records, of which 22 studies met the inclusion criteria. Bias was represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon, with social bias identified most frequently (21/22 studies), followed by algorithmic bias (16/22 studies), structural bias (14/22 studies), and design-related bias (12/22 studies). Patient empowerment was most frequently addressed through involvement in care (n=13), followed by health literacy (n=9) and trust and assurance (n=7), whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life domains were addressed less frequently. Digital divide–related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers reported most frequently. Seven studies considered 2 or more social or structural dimensions of disadvantage. Although many studies discussed approaches that could mitigate bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent. Conclusions Patient-related consequences of bias in medical AI extend beyond algorithmic performance and are reflected in access, understanding, trust, and involvement in care. Broader empowerment dimensions, multidimensional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated mitigation strategies remain comparatively underexplored.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority. Methods The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation. Results The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated. Discussion Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.

items.abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

items.abstract_text: As digital technology becomes more deeply embedded in education, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly present in junior high school students' daily learning. This paper explores the "scaffolding" role of GenAI in students' self-regulated learning (SRL) and its possible influence on enhancing academic self-efficacy. Based on Zimmerman's cyclical phase model of SRL and learning scaffolding theory, the study systematically deduces the human-AI interaction process. The analysis suggests that GenAI acts as planning, monitoring, and reflective feedback scaffolds across the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases, effectively addressing the lack of personalized support in traditional autonomous learning. Furthermore, GenAI assistance contributes to the internalization of academic self-efficacy by accumulating direct mastery experiences and alleviating trial-and-error anxiety. Acknowledging the potential risks of cognitive offloading and academic misconduct associated with GenAI dependency, the paper proposes coping strategies such as cultivating students' critical GenAI literacy and implementing dynamic scaffold fading. This research provides theoretical support and practical guidance for educators to optimize GenAI-assisted self-regulated learning environments.

items.abstract_text: Against the backdrop of generative AI emerging as a core strategic asset for major powers, the rhetorical tropes of national security and industrial competitiveness are subject to strategic manipulation by divergent domestic actors. The deregulatory camp within the White House invokes industrial competitiveness to roll back security-focused executive orders; the security faction in Congress expands chip export controls in the name of national defense; state-level authorities counter federal overreach through consumer protection mandates; and Silicon Valley deploys a two-pronged lobbying strategy. Taking the 2023-2026 policy pendulum and BIS chip regulations as its analytical case, this paper demonstrates that domestic contestation spills over globally through transmission channels. This has produced a global AI governance landscape defined by fragmentation, hollowed-out soft law processes, and a three-bloc divide across the U.S., the EU, and China, while the shortening commitment half-life of U.S. policy positions has inflated the costs of multilateral cooperation. The study also identifies limited positive spillover effects. In response, the paper puts forward targeted strategies. The conclusion argues that U.S. internal regulatory divisions constitute a mechanism that externalizes domestic political costs as global governance uncertainty. Understanding this mechanism is a prerequisite for reshaping the multilateral AI order.

items.abstract_text: With AI agents increasingly involved in teamwork, whether AI can substitute human collaboration has become a heated topic in academia. Large-model-driven agents are now capable of participating in team brainstorming, task coordination, and collaborative problem-solving, and knowledge-intensive industries are beginning to form a large number of human-machine hybrid teams. Existing research mostly relies on theoretical reasoning and lacks empirical perceptual data from front-line practitioners. Drawing on a questionnaire survey of 158 employees with cross-industry teamwork experience, this paper explores practitioners' perceptions regarding the substitution of human collaborative behaviors by AI. The results show that AI can only partially substitute procedural and rule-oriented collaborative tasks, whereas social-emotional communication, conflict mediation and value judgment remain irreplaceable human strengths. Position, work experience and AI familiarity jointly shape individual perceptions of the substitution boundary. Most practitioners regard AI as an auxiliary tool rather than a leader of team collaboration. This study provides a practical reference for enterprises applying AI collaboration tools.

Implications of the findings are discussed.
